name: Mexico City Benito Juárez International Airport
before:
Mexico's busiest airport, 5 km east of downtown Mexico City, and as of 2025 third busiest in Latin America. It handled 44,605,576 passengers in 2025 across more than 25 airlines and over 100 destinations.

The constraint to understand is capacity. The airport operates at full capacity and is one of the busiest two-runway airports in the world, with 850 aircraft movements a day. Its two parallel runways sit less than 300 metres apart, which rules out simultaneous operations, so the airport cannot simply add flights. Delays are structural, not occasional.

Altitude matters here too. At 2,230 metres the airport is classified as hot and high, where thinner air reduces aircraft performance.

There are two passenger terminals. They are not close together, so confirm which one a client departs from.

Mexico City has two other airports, Toluca and Felipe Ángeles, which between them take some of the overflow.

It is named after Benito Juárez, the nineteenth century president.
after:
Mexico's busiest airport and one of the busiest in Latin America, about 5 km east of downtown Mexico City. It handled 44,605,576 passengers in 2025, 1.7 per cent fewer than in 2024, and the airport's own list names 22 airlines.

The airport runs at full capacity, with about 850 aircraft movements a day on two parallel runways only about 300 metres apart. It sits at 2,230 metres above sea level.

The two passenger terminals are linked by a train that needs a boarding pass, so confirm which one a client departs from.

Another airport, Felipe Ángeles, opened in 2022 to share Mexico City's traffic, and all-cargo flights moved there in 2023.

It is named after Benito Juárez, the nineteenth century president.

claims.claim: Mexico's busiest airport
claims.note: AICM counted 44,605,576 passengers in 2025. ASUR, citing AFAC, says Cancún was Mexico's second busiest airport in 2025, with 29,345.5 thousand, so Mexico City is first. AICM's own capacity study calls it the country's main point of air connectivity.

claims.claim: FCDO: volcanic ash has disrupted flights; use authorised airport taxis
claims.why: Held back: the FCDO says ash from Popocatépetl has previously disrupted air travel and caused cancellations at Benito Juárez International Airport, and that at airports only authorised pre-paid taxis should be used. Mexico City is not among the areas it advises against (updated 22 September 2026). A warning with nothing in the old text to replace.

claims.claim: direct flights from Heathrow
claims.why: Held back, for Andy: the UK Civil Aviation Authority counted 293,512 passengers between Heathrow and Mexico City in 2025 (297,852 in 2024), all on scheduled flights, and British Airways is on the airport's own airline list. The only direct UK link; the old text says nothing about UK flights, so there is nothing to replace.
